lessons.title: Sector Rotation: Which Nifty Sectors Lead in Each Phase

body.text: Not every rupee of a market rally comes from the same sectors. As the cycle turns, equity leadership rotates in a fairly predictable order, and reading that order is one of the highest-value skills an equity investor can build.

children.text: Chapter 1 gave you the four phases and the growth-inflation grid. This chapter puts them to work, starting with equities, the asset class most investors touch first. Within equities, the single most useful application of everything you've learned so far is sector rotation: certain groups of Nifty sectors tend to lead at certain points in the cycle, and certain groups tend to lag at those same points.
Cyclicals vs Defensives: The Basic Split

body.title: The two broad camps every sector falls into

columns.label: Cyclical sectors
points: Earnings swing hard with the economy: banks, auto, realty, metals, capital goods
Demand is often big-ticket or credit-financed, so it's the first to freeze when rates rise or confidence drops
Tend to fall hardest in a contraction and rally hardest off a trough
Valuations (P/E) often look cheapest right before they turn, and expensive right before they roll over

columns.label: Defensive sectors
points: Demand is fairly inelastic: FMCG, pharma, utilities
People keep buying soap, medicine, and electricity in a slowdown
Earnings and share prices fall less in a contraction
Tend to lag badly once cyclicals take over in a strong recovery

body.caption: Which Nifty sectors typically lead, phase by phase

cells: Banks, NBFCs, PSU banks, auto, realty
Rate cuts feed through, the most beaten-down and most rate-sensitive names re-rate fastest as confidence returns
Capex picks up, order books fill, and commodity demand starts rising with the broader economy
Inflation runs hot, and pricing power shifts toward resource producers rather than resource users
Demand for staples, medicine, and power is fairly inelastic, so earnings hold up better as discretionary spending falls

body.text: This rotation clock is just the growth-inflation grid from Chapter 1 applied inside the equity market. Early expansion (rising growth, falling inflation) favours rate-sensitive cyclicals. Overheat (rising growth, rising inflation) favours commodity producers. Contraction hands leadership to whatever people keep buying regardless of the cycle.

children.text: How This Played Out on the Nifty: 2020 to 2024

During the Covid crash of February to March 2020, the contraction phase, Nifty Pharma fell far less than the broader market, while Nifty Bank and Nifty Realty each fell by more than 40%. Defensives did exactly what the framework predicts: they held up while cyclicals were hit hardest.

Then came FY21, the trough-into-expansion phase covered in Chapter 1. Leadership flipped completely. The most beaten-down cyclicals, metals, PSU banks, realty, and auto, delivered the biggest gains of the year, while FMCG, which had barely fallen in the crash, ended up the year's laggard.

body.title: Nifty sectoral index returns, FY21 (approximate, rounded)

body.text: Pharma is the sector to watch here. It was one of the more resilient sectors during the crash itself, and it still posted a decent, positive FY21 return, but it finished well behind the cyclicals that had been crushed the hardest. The sector that protects you on the way down is rarely the sector that makes you the most money on the way back up. That is rotation, in one chart.

children.text: Through 2021 and into 2022, as growth stayed strong but inflation climbed, the baton passed again: Nifty Metal and Nifty Energy remained among the strongest performers on rising commodity prices, while Nifty IT and Nifty Realty, both sensitive to rising interest rates, faded as the RBI and other central banks began tightening. By 2023 and 2024, with inflation cooling and a broad domestic capex and credit cycle underway, leadership widened out again into banks, auto, and capital-goods names, a classic mid-expansion pattern.

body.text: Rotation is a tendency, not a schedule. Government policy can override the clock: the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme and a multi-year defence and railways capex push kept capital goods and industrial stocks strong through periods when the pure cycle framework alone would not have called for it. Company-specific and policy-specific stories can extend or shorten a sector's leadership well beyond what the phase alone predicts.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: Over the last two quarters, Nifty Metal and Nifty Energy have outperformed the broader Nifty 50, while Nifty FMCG and Nifty Pharma have lagged. GDP growth is still positive but inflation is rising. Which phase does this pattern most likely reflect?
body.explanation: Commodity and energy leadership, alongside underperforming defensives, combined with rising growth and rising inflation, is the classic overheat signature: resource producers benefit from pricing power while the broader market's appetite for defensives fades.

body.title: Reading a Sector Leaderboard
body.scenario: You pull up the one-year sectoral index returns and see this ranking, best to worst: Nifty Bank, Nifty Auto, Nifty Realty, Nifty Capital Goods, Nifty 50, Nifty IT, Nifty Metal, Nifty Pharma, Nifty FMCG. GDP growth has been accelerating for several quarters and inflation has been easing.
body.prompt: Which phase does this leaderboard most resemble, and which sectors would you expect to take over leadership if the economy moves into the next phase?
body.modelAnswer: Rate-sensitive cyclicals (banks, auto, realty) leading with capital goods close behind, while metals, pharma, and FMCG lag, fits a mid-expansion phase: growth accelerating, inflation still benign, credit and construction-linked demand strengthening. If the economy moves into overheat next, growth staying strong but inflation starting to rise, you would expect the framework to favour metals, energy, and other commodity producers taking over the top of the leaderboard, with capital-goods and industrial names likely staying in the mix a while longer as capex continues, and the currently lagging FMCG and pharma names staying near the bottom until the cycle eventually turns down.

cards.definition: The tendency for equity market leadership to shift between groups of sectors as the business cycle moves through its phases.
A sector whose earnings and share prices swing heavily with the economy, such as banks, auto, realty, and metals.
A sector with fairly inelastic demand, such as FMCG, pharma, and utilities, whose earnings hold up better in a slowdown.
Public sector bank; the Nifty PSU Bank index is one of the most rate- and credit-cycle-sensitive sectoral indices on the NSE.

body.text: Sectoral index returns in this lesson are rounded, approximate, and drawn from widely reported figures for the periods discussed, provided for education only. Sector rotation is a historical tendency, not a rule, and individual stocks within a sector can behave very differently from the sectoral index. Nothing here is investment advice; consult a SEBI registered investment adviser for advice on your own portfolio.

points: Equity sectors split broadly into cyclicals (banks, auto, realty, metals), which swing hard with the economy, and defensives (FMCG, pharma, utilities), whose demand stays fairly steady
The sector rotation clock maps directly onto the growth-inflation grid: early expansion favours rate-sensitive cyclicals, overheat favours commodity producers, and contraction favours defensives

In the FY20 crash, defensives like Nifty Pharma fell far less than cyclicals; in the FY21 recovery, the hardest-hit cyclicals like Nifty Metal, PSU Bank, and Realty led by a wide margin, while FMCG lagged
The sector that protects your portfolio in a downturn is often not the sector that drives your returns in the recovery that follows
Government policy, such as the PLI scheme and a multi-year defence and infrastructure capex push, can keep a sector's leadership going well beyond what the pure cycle framework alone would predict
Use sector rotation to understand which sectors have the wind behind them, not as a precise timing tool for entries and exits
